Use Futur II for assumptions about the past (Er wird es vergessen haben = he's probably forgotten).

“virt … HAH-ben”: stress on the participle and on the final auxiliary.
1. Assumptions about the present: Futur I + wohl
You learnt this in chapter 21: “werden” + infinitive + “wohl” = an assumption about NOW:
His battery has probably run out. (it's flat now)
2. Assumptions about the past: Futur II
Futur II = werden + participle + haben / sein (at the end). In theory it's the “future perfect”, but in practice it's almost always used for assumptions about the PAST:
Er wird zum Friedhof gefahren sein.
He'll have gone to the cemetery.
Sie wird den Bus verpasst haben.
Recipe: take the Perfekt, put “wird” in position 2 and the auxiliary (haben / sein) at the end. “Er ist gegangen” → “Er wird gegangen sein”.
The real future meaning is rare: “Bis Freitag werde ich das Buch gelesen haben.” = By Friday I will have read the book.
3. How sure you are: the modals
The modals also express assumptions, with different degrees of certainty:
Er muss im Park sein. (I'm almost sure)
Er könnte im Park sein. (it's possible)
Er kann nicht im Park sein. (it can't be)
For the past: modal + participle + haben / sein: “Er muss zum Friedhof gefahren sein.” “Sie könnte gestürzt sein.”
“Er muss im Park sein” can also express an obligation (he has to be there), depending on the context. “Das kann nicht sein!” = That can't be! is a very common expression.

They took the M10, Mara, Lena and Andrei, and rode through Prenzlauer Berg towards Friedrichshain. It was a warm June evening, and the streets were full of people sitting in cafés and eating ice cream. Lena looked out of the window the whole way, as if she might spot her grandfather somewhere on the pavement. “He's probably got lost,” she said quietly. “He's probably sitting somewhere and doesn't know where he is any more.”

Mara took her hand. She was a nurse. She knew that old people are sometimes confused, that they forget routes they have travelled for fifty years. But she also knew Ludwig. “That can't be,” she said. “For forty years Ludwig knew every street in this city. Maybe he forgets to charge his phone. But he never forgets a route. He'll know exactly where he is.”

Andrei said nothing. He was thinking of his own grandfather in Sibiu, who had died three years ago. He too used to disappear for hours sometimes, and the family always suspected the worst. And every time they found him in the same place: at the cemetery, at his wife's grave, with a newspaper and a flask of tea. “Old people don't disappear,” Andrei said at last. “They just go to places we don't think of. He'll have had a reason. He always has a reason.”

The tram stopped at the Am Friedrichshain stop. They got off. Lena's phone rang: it was Jakob. “Have you found him?” “Not yet,” said Lena. “But Mara thinks she knows where he is.” Jakob was silent for a moment. “If Mara thinks so, then it'll be true,” he said then. “She found me too, back then on the stairs, when I didn't even know yet that I wanted to be found.” Lena couldn't help smiling in spite of everything.

The Volkspark Friedrichshain was big, green and full of people. Young people were lying on the grass, children were playing football, an old man was selling ice cream from a bicycle. The Fairy-Tale Fountain was at the entrance to the park, a large old fountain of white stone, with figures from the Brothers Grimm's fairy tales all around the water: Little Red Riding Hood, Hansel and Gretel, Puss in Boots. The water splashed down over several steps.

Lena went on ahead, past families, dogs and bicycles. Mara followed her, Andrei stayed a few steps behind, looking around. Someone was sitting on every bench: a young couple having an argument, a woman with a pram, two old men playing chess. “That must be him,” Lena called out once, pointing at a man in a grey hat. But when they got closer, it was a stranger who looked at them in surprise. “He must be around here somewhere,” Mara said calmly. “I'm sure.”

And there, on a bench at the edge of the fountain, in the shade of a big lime tree, sat Ludwig. Fritz was lying at his feet, asleep. Ludwig had his eyes closed and his face turned towards the evening sun. Next to him on the bench lay a single red rose.

Lena stopped. For one terrible moment she thought he was dead. He wasn't moving. Then Fritz opened one eye, saw her and started wagging his tail. And Ludwig opened his eyes and said, without any surprise: “At last. I thought you'd come. Mara will have worked it out, won't she?”
Grandpa! We were so worried! You've been gone for seven hours! Your phone is off!
My phone? It'll be flat. I forgot to charge it. I'm sorry, Lena. Today I just wanted… to be with her.
Lena sat down next to him and hugged him, and Ludwig let her, which rarely happened. Mara and Andrei sat down on the bench opposite and waited. After a while, Ludwig began to tell his story.

In the summer of 1972, on an evening like this, I sat exactly here. On this bench, or on one that used to be here. Ingrid had a book with her, of course. I had my guitar. I played her a song, a bad song I had written myself. She laughed. Not at the song, she said, but because I was so nervous. And then she closed the book and kissed me. I never dared. She did it.

He laughed quietly. Lena was crying. Andrei was looking at the splashing water and thinking of a bakery at four in the morning, of a question that he wouldn't have dared to ask either, if Lena hadn't asked it first.

She would have turned eighty-one today. In the morning I went to the cemetery. Then I came here by tram and sat down on this bench. I only wanted to stay for an hour. But then I talked to her, and time went by, and Fritz fell asleep, and so did I, I think. You'll have thought I was lost.
Lena thought so. I didn't. I knew you weren't lost. You were just with someone you miss.

For a while nobody said anything. A little girl came to the fountain, threw a coin into the water and made a wish, with her eyes closed, very serious. Ludwig smiled when he saw her. “Ingrid used to do that too,” he said. “Every time we were here. I'd ask her what she wished for and she never told me. She said otherwise it wouldn't come true. I suspect she wished for something for us. For the family. For the house. And do you know what, Lena? It must have worked.”

Ludwig looked at Mara for a long time. Then he nodded. “You're right. And do you know what? She told me something today. Not really, of course. But I know what she would have said. She would have said: Ludwig, you old donkey, you can't sit on a bench all day. Go home. There are people there who love you.”

Lena laughed through her tears. “That sounds just like Grandma.” She searched in her bag, found a coin and gave it to her grandfather. Ludwig looked at the coin for a long time, then threw it into the water, closed his eyes and moved his lips. “What did you wish for, Grandpa?” Lena asked. Ludwig shook his head and smiled. “I'm not telling. Otherwise it won't come true. But I can tell you this: it has something to do with Andrei.” Andrei blushed, and Mara couldn't help laughing.

He stood up, slowly, leaning on his walking stick, and Andrei helped him. He left the red rose on the bench, at the edge of the fountain, where the stone Hansel and Gretel had been waiting for a gingerbread house for a hundred years. They walked to the tram together, four people and an old dog, slowly, in the golden evening light. Lena held her grandfather's hand the whole way. And that evening Andrei wrote a new story in the brown notebook: “The Fairy-Tale Fountain, 1972 and 2031.”

The Volkspark Friedrichshain was opened in 1848 and is the oldest public park in Berlin.
At the entrance is the Fairy-Tale Fountain, built in 1913. Figures from the Brothers Grimm's fairy tales stand around the water.
There are two hills in the park. They'll probably surprise many visitors: they are the rubble of houses destroyed in the war.
Today, in summer, people sit there in the sun. Many probably don't know what's underneath them.
Older Berliners say that they fell in love here for the first time. The park must know a lot of stories.
